difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY - one concept (Bayes' theorem, with the law of total probability for the denominator) applied by direct substitution of the given prior and likelihoods, with routine arithmetic (0.24/0.31); about 1 to 1.5 minutes for a prepared student.
stem:
A clinic specializes in testing for a disease $\mathsf{D}$. The result of the test can be either positive or negative.

A study revealed that if a person suffers from the disease $\mathsf{D}$, the test result in that clinic comes out positive 80% of the time, and negative 20% of the time. If a person is not suffering from the disease $\mathsf{D}$, the test comes out positive 10% of the time and negative 90% of the time. It is also known that among the general population, the disease $\mathsf{D}$ occurs in 30% of the individuals.

If a person tests positive for $\mathsf{D}$ in that clinic, the probability that he/she actually suffers from the disease $\mathsf{D}$ is __________ . (Rounded off to **two** decimal places)

solution.quick: Bayes' theorem. With prior $P(\mathsf{D}) = 0.3$ and likelihoods $P(+ \mid \mathsf{D}) = 0.8$, $P(+ \mid \mathsf{D}^c) = 0.1$, a positive result has total probability $P(+) = 0.8(0.3) + 0.1(0.7) = 0.24 + 0.07 = 0.31$. Hence $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +) = 0.24/0.31 = 24/31 \approx 0.774$, which rounds to **0.77**.

steps.title: Name the events and read off the data
steps.body:
Let $\mathsf{D}$ be the event that a person has the disease, $\mathsf{D}^c$ that they do not, and $+$ / $-$ that the test is positive / negative.

| Quantity | Meaning | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $P(\mathsf{D})$ | prior: prevalence in the population | $0.30$ |
| $P(\mathsf{D}^c)$ | $1 - P(\mathsf{D})$ | $0.70$ |
| $P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})$ | positive given diseased (sensitivity) | $0.80$ |
| $P(+ \mid \mathsf{D}^c)$ | positive given not diseased (false-positive rate) | $0.10$ |

The 20% and 90% figures are the complements $P(- \mid \mathsf{D}) = 0.2$ and $P(- \mid \mathsf{D}^c) = 0.9$; they are consistent with the positive rates but not needed. The question gives the test behaviour in the direction "disease $\to$ result" and asks for the reverse direction, $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +)$.

steps.title: Total probability of a positive result
steps.body:
A positive result comes either from a person who has $\mathsf{D}$ or from one who does not. These two cases are disjoint and cover the whole population, so by the law of total probability

$$
P(+) = P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})\,P(\mathsf{D}) + P(+ \mid \mathsf{D}^c)\,P(\mathsf{D}^c) = (0.8)(0.3) + (0.1)(0.7) = 0.24 + 0.07 = 0.31.
$$

The first term, $0.24 = P(\mathsf{D} \cap +)$, is the probability of having the disease **and** testing positive (true positives); the second, $0.07 = P(\mathsf{D}^c \cap +)$, is the false positives.

steps.title: Apply Bayes' theorem
steps.body:
$$
P(\mathsf{D} \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})\,P(\mathsf{D})}{P(+)} = \frac{0.24}{0.31} = \frac{24}{31} = 0.774193\ldots
$$

In words: of all positive results, the fraction that come from truly diseased people is $0.24$ out of $0.31$.

steps.title: Round and sanity-check
steps.body:
Rounded off to two decimal places, $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +) = 0.7742 \approx 0.77$, which lies in the official range 0.76 to 0.78.

Sanity check: the posterior $0.77$ is much higher than the prior $0.30$, as it should be, since a positive result is evidence for the disease. It is still well short of 1, because 7 of every 31 positive results come from the larger group of people without the disease.

solution.teaching:
**Conditional probability has a direction.** $P(A \mid B)$ is the probability of $A$ among the cases where $B$ happened. Diagnostic studies usually report the "disease $\to$ test" direction: among diseased people, how often is the test positive ($P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})$, the *sensitivity*), and among healthy people, how often is it positive ($P(+ \mid \mathsf{D}^c)$, the *false-positive rate*). A patient with a positive result wants the opposite direction: how likely am I to be ill, $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +)$? Bayes' theorem converts one direction into the other.

**Deriving Bayes' theorem.** The joint probability can be written in two ways, $P(\mathsf{D} \cap +) = P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})\,P(\mathsf{D}) = P(\mathsf{D} \mid +)\,P(+)$. Solving for the unknown gives $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +) = P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})\,P(\mathsf{D}) / P(+)$. The denominator comes from the law of total probability: split the positives by where they came from, $P(+) = P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})P(\mathsf{D}) + P(+ \mid \mathsf{D}^c)P(\mathsf{D}^c)$.

**The natural-frequency picture.** Imagine 1000 people. 300 have the disease, and 80% of them, 240 people, test positive. 700 do not, and 10% of them, 70 people, also test positive. Of the 310 positives, 240 are truly ill, so $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +) = 240/310 = 24/31$. The formula is exactly this counting written with probabilities.

**Why the prior matters.** With the same test but a rare disease (1% prevalence), the posterior would be $0.008/(0.008 + 0.099) \approx 0.07$: most positives would be false alarms from the huge healthy group. Here the prevalence is a high 30%, so the posterior is large.

**Connecting to this question.** Prior 0.3, likelihoods 0.8 and 0.1: true positives weigh $0.24$ against $0.07$ false positives, so $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +) = 0.24/0.31 \approx 0.77$.
solution.shortcut: Use natural frequencies per 100 people: 30 have $\mathsf{D}$, and 24 of them test positive; 70 do not, and 7 of them test positive. So $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +) = 24/(24 + 7) = 24/31 \approx 0.77$.
solution.commonTrap: Answering $0.80$, which is $P(+ \mid \mathsf{D})$, instead of the asked $P(\mathsf{D} \mid +)$ (confusing a conditional probability with its inverse). Other slips: reporting the joint probability $0.24 = P(\mathsf{D} \cap +)$ without dividing by $P(+)$, leaving the $0.07$ false positives from people without the disease out of the denominator, or putting the negative rates (20%, 90%) into the total-probability sum.

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
from fractions import Fraction as F
p_D, sens, fpr = F(3, 10), F(8, 10), F(1, 10)   # P(D), P(+|D), P(+|not D)
p_pos = sens*p_D + fpr*(1 - p_D)                 # total probability of a positive test
post = sens*p_D / p_pos                          # Bayes: P(D|+)
print(p_pos, post, float(post), round(float(post), 2))   # 31/100 24/31 0.7741935... 0.77
assert p_pos == F(31, 100) and post == F(24, 31)
assert 0.76 <= round(float(post), 2) <= 0.78     # official key 0.76 to 0.78
# natural-frequency cross-check on 1000 people
sick_pos, healthy_pos = 1000*0.3*0.8, 1000*0.7*0.1   # 240, 70
assert abs(sick_pos/(sick_pos + healthy_pos) - float(post)) < 1e-12
# Monte Carlo sanity check
import random
random.seed(0); pos = sick = 0
for _ in range(1_000_000):
    d = random.random() < 0.3
    t = random.random() < (0.8 if d else 0.1)
    if t: pos += 1; sick += d
print('MC P(D|+) =', round(sick/pos, 4))
answerVerification.notes: Law of total probability: P(+) = 0.8(0.3) + 0.1(0.7) = 0.31. Bayes: P(D|+) = 0.24/0.31 = 24/31 = 0.7742, which rounds to 0.77. Exact rational arithmetic, a natural-frequency cross-check (240 of 310 positives per 1000 people) and a 1,000,000-trial Monte Carlo simulation (0.7747) agree. 0.77 lies within the official key range 0.76 to 0.78.
